title: The Outcasts of Poker Flat
focus: moral worth found among those society rejects

teacherSummary.text: In 1850, a vigilance committee in the mining camp of Poker Flat expels gambler John Oakhurst, 'The Duchess', Mother Shipton and drunken Uncle Billy. On the trail they meet innocent young Tom Simson and his fiancée Piney. Snowed in, Uncle Billy steals the mules. Mother Shipton starves herself to save food for Piney; Tom goes for help. Oakhurst shoots himself under a pine; the Duchess and Piney die in each other's arms.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “the deuce of clubs pinned to the bark with a bowie-knife” slowly and put it in my own words: Oakhurst's body is found under a tree with the deuce of clubs fastened to the bark by a knife, carrying his last words. Next, craft. I notice the details are all gambling and frontier tools, a card and a bowie-knife, rather than anything religious. The strongest word is “deuce”: a deuce is the lowest card in the deck, so he is saying his luck ran out completely. Then, effect. Why does Oakhurst leave a playing card as his own grave marker? My answer: Oakhurst leaves a playing card as his own grave marker because it sums up his life as a gambler's losing hand; the card is a grim joke and a confession, and it is how he chooses to be remembered.
